figures.caption: Figure 1: Latency breakdown on SIFT100M under a memory budget of 0.4× dataset size with 𝑇 ∈ {2, 4, 8} threads. (a) Latency decomposed into I/O only, CPU-I/O overlap, and CPU only components. (b) Breakdown of total query latency into CPU meaningful work and CPU idle time at 𝑇 = 8 threads.

Figure 7: Look-ahead search with𝑊 = 2. Green nodes are cached in memory; white nodes are on-disk; blue nodes have been explored. Yellow dashed boxes mark the top-𝑊 unvisited vectors inspected by the persistence check. Red circles indicate persistent nodes.
Figure 13: Recall@10 vs. latency (top row) and recall@10 vs. throughput (bottom row) on SIFT1B and SpaceV1B under a memory budget of 0.3× the dataset size.

Figure 12: Recall@10 vs. latency (top row) and recall@10 vs. throughput (bottom row) on three 100M-scale datasets under a memory budget of 0.5× the dataset size. Lower latency and higher throughput are better.

Figure 2: Illustration of greedy search on a proximity graph with candidate pool size 𝐿 = 3. The search traverses from the entry point toward the query, updating the candidate pool at each step until convergence.

Figure 3: Illustration of processing vectors cached inmemory before issuing I/O on a proximity graph with candidate pool size 𝐿 = 3. Blue arrows indicate expansions that require I/O; red arrows indicate expansions of vectors cached in memory requiring no I/O. Red-circled nodes are cached in memory.
Figure 5: System overview of LAANN. The DRAM region holds three purpose-built structures; the SSD stores the page-level disk graph. Numbers indicate the search flow.
